chapters.name: Reading Comprehension
chapters.introduction: Reading comprehension tests the ability to understand and interpret unseen prose passages. Questions target main idea, inferencing, vocabulary in context, and factual detail.
chapters.whyItMatters: 15-20 marks. Both factual and inferential questions appear. Strong comprehension skills boost performance across all English sections.

topics.name: Factual Questions
topics.explanation: Factual questions ask what a passage directly states. Locate the relevant sentence, restate the answer in your own words or in a complete sentence. Use clue words from the question to skim the passage.
topics.examTip: Do not add outside knowledge. All answers exist in the passage.

topics.name: Inferential Questions
topics.explanation: Inferential questions require reading between the lines. The answer is implied, not directly stated. Use clues from the text, tone, and context to arrive at the logical conclusion.
topics.examTip: Base inferences only on the text. Personal opinions cause wrong answers.

topics.name: Poems and Stories Interpretation
topics.explanation: Literary texts require identifying theme, moral, tone, and figures of speech (simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration). Poems use compressed language; stories carry narrative morals.
topics.examTip: Theme = universal lesson; Plot = what happened.

chapters.name: Letter Writing
chapters.introduction: Formal and informal letters are regularly tested. Formal letters include complaint, application, and inquiry. Informal letters are to friends or family.
chapters.whyItMatters: 10-12 marks. Format marks are easy to secure. Content, tone, and format together determine the score.

topics.name: Formal Letter
topics.explanation: Formal letter format: Sender's Address → Date → Receiver's Address → Subject → Salutation → Body (3 paragraphs) → Closing → Signature. Use formal, polite language throughout.
keyPoints: Sign off: Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully
topics.examTip: Losing format marks is avoidable — memorise the structure and reproduce it correctly.

topics.name: Essay Writing
topics.explanation: Essays have Introduction → 2-3 Body Paragraphs → Conclusion. Common topics: pollution, technology, education, tourism in Nepal. Use topic sentences to open each paragraph.
topics.examTip: Spend 2 minutes planning before writing. Organised essays score higher.

chapters.name: Tense
chapters.introduction: Tenses define the time of an action. SEE tests all 12 tenses with a focus on Present Perfect, Past Simple, and Future forms through gap-fills and sentence transformation.
chapters.whyItMatters: Grammar carries 35-40 marks total. Tense errors are the most common in writing.

topics.name: 12 Tenses Overview
topics.explanation: Present (Simple / Continuous / Perfect / Perfect Continuous), Past (Simple / Continuous / Perfect / Perfect Continuous), Future (Simple / Continuous / Perfect / Perfect Continuous). Each tense has a specific time signal.
topics.examTip: Identify the time expression first. It will tell you the tense.

topics.name: Active and Passive Voice
topics.explanation: Voice transformation changes focus from doer (active) to receiver (passive). Formula: Object → Subject, Verb → be + past participle, Subject → by + Agent (optional). Tense of 'be' must match original tense.
keyPoints: Passive: Object + be(tense) + V3 + by Subject
Modal passives: Subject + modal + be + V3
topics.examTip: Change both the verb form and pronoun case (he → him) simultaneously.
topics.formula: Active: She writes a letter → Passive: A letter is written by her

topics.name: Direct and Indirect Narration
topics.explanation: Narration converts quoted speech (direct) to reported speech (indirect). Rules: (1) Reporting verb changes, (2) Tense backshifts, (3) Pronouns change, (4) Time expressions change (today → that day, yesterday → the day before).
keyPoints: Tense backshift: is → was, will → would
topics.examTip: Write out the pronoun and tense changes on your scratch paper before writing the answer.
